item.title: Universities, schools nationwide use Thanksgiving as chance to promote 'Day of Mourning' and decolonization
item.description: Campus Thanksgiving events have been reframed as a "National Day of Mourning" for Indigenous remembrance, with Salem State and Pratt citing historical harm.
item.content:encoded:
Thanksgiving is a day of celebration and spending time with family for the vast majority of Americans, but for several students on college campuses across the country, the national holiday is a source of anguish that is being expressed in the form of protests and counter-programming events.

On Nov. 18, George Washington University hosted an event called "Breaking Bread: The Cost of Celebration" that was described as a chance for students to examine Thanksgiving, Christmas and Independence Day through an intersectional lens, including experiences of "belonging, exclusion, cultural erasure, and historical harm."

"Through facilitated dialogue and shared reflection, students will engage in meaningful conversations about historical memory, social responsibility, and the complexities of celebrating within a diverse society," the student life event description read.

At the University of Wisconsin at Milwaukee, the American Indian Student Center & Electa Quinney Institute for American Indian Education hosted a Nov. 17 event called "AlterNative Giving," which was described as "a community gathering that offers a meaningful alternative to the traditional Thanksgiving narrative. Instead of focusing on colonial histories, we come together to honor Indigenous ways of knowing, being, and giving."

TRUMP DEI CRACKDOWN ‘MISSES CORE IDEOLOGY' AND MUST TARGET LINGERING DANGER ON CAMPUSES, WATCHDOG WARNS

Salem State University promoted an event that labeled Thanksgiving as a "National Day of Mourning" and told students the land they are being educated on was stolen from Indigenous people.

"The land occupied by Salem State University is part of the traditional and ancestral homeland of the Massachusett tribe," the school’s website posted. "We acknowledge the genocide and forced removal of the Massachusett tribe and their kin from their summer home in Nâmkek."

CALIFORNIA COLLEGE LECTURER REMOVED AFTER ERUPTING AT STUDENT OVER QUESTION ON NATIVE AMERICANS

A review of university calendars found several examples lamenting the downsides of Thanksgiving, including Occidental College, which said the holiday is a "reminder of settler colonialism and its devastating impact on Indigenous individuals, communities and tribes."

The Pratt Institute lists "National Day of Mourning" as an occasion for Indigenous remembrance and reflection, and the University at Albany lists the holiday as "National Day of Mourning/Thanksgiving."

The colonial messaging around Thanksgiving isn't limited to universities but is also occurring at elementary and high schools, including in Loudoun County, Virginia, where a parent recently pushed back in an interview with Fox News about school lesson plans teaching children that Thanksgiving is a "Day of Mourning."

On its website, the San Diego County Office of Education explained that "November is Native American Heritage Month, a time to honor the diversity, history, and living cultures of Native peoples. It is also the month when Thanksgiving is observed in the United States, a holiday that carries very different meanings for different people, including many Native communities."

Oregon’s Bethel School District links to a "Decolonizing Thanksgiving: A Toolkit for Combatting Racism in Schools" on its official Equity, Access & Inclusion webpage. Listed under teaching resources, the toolkit appears alongside material about honoring Native peoples on Thanksgiving.

item.title: Chris Van Hollen gains celebrity donor backing as Fonda, De Niro and more support ditching Schumer in letter
item.description: Jane Fonda, Robert De Niro and more celebrities and Democratic donors said they supported Sen. Chris Van Hollen over Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader.
item.content:encoded:
A group of about 35 Hollywood stars and Democratic donors signed a letter Tuesday supporting Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., over Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for Senate Majority Leader.

"The Senate Democratic leader will be chosen behind closed doors, by secret ballot," the letter said, according to The New York Times. "No senator will ever have to tell voters, or us, how they voted. We believe a decision this consequential deserves public accountability."

Jane Fonda, Robert De Niro, Chelsea Handler, Marisa Tomei, Padma Lakshmi and David Mandel are among the signatories of the letter, the Times reported.

SCHUMER'S FORMER ALLY MOUNTS LEADERSHIP CHALLENGE AS DEMOCRATS FACE RARE INTERNAL POWER STRUGGLE

Morris Pearl, a former BlackRock executive, and V, born Eve Ensler, the author of "The Vagina Monologues," also signed the letter, according to the Times. Both had donated to Schumer in the past.

They say they donated or helped to raise about $23 million for Democratic candidates in House and Senate races this election cycle. Van Hollen announced he would challenge Schumer earlier this month.

The donors and celebrities argue that re-electing Schumer was not what the Democratic electorate wanted, according to the Times.

"This is an opportunity. This is a window," Handler said, according to the Times. "We need to, like, get the ball and run with it. And I don’t believe that Chuck Schumer is going to do that."

MARK RUFFALO DOUBLES DOWN ON CALL TO OUST SCHUMER OVER 'ENTRENCHED RELIGIOUS BELIEFS AND LOYALTIES'

Schumer's office did not immediately return Fox News Digital's request for comment.

The group of donors expressed frustration over Schumer's constrained support for progressive candidates in the midterm elections, the Times reported.

"Americans voted for the change necessary to fight the corruption, cruelty and policies of Trump and his Epstein-class cronies," De Niro said in a statement to the Times. "That’s why I’m supporting change in Senate leadership."

De Niro also called Van Hollen a "fierce fighter."

SCHUMER FACES MUTINY FROM NEWLY ELECTED SENATE DEMS AS PARTY PREPARES TO SEIZE POWER

The race for majority leader will be contested for the first time in three decades, and both Schumer and Van Hollen believe they have or can get the 28 votes needed to claim the mantle of Democratic leader and become majority leader.

Neither senator has publicly locked down enough support to eclipse the magic number.

BERNIE SANDERS SAYS HE WON'T BACK SCHUMER AS PUSH FOR NEW LEADERSHIP GAINS STEAM

Van Hollen has the support of Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., Sens.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., Peggy Flanagan, D-Minn., and Troy Jackson, D-Maine, as well as Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., and Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore.

Slotkin announced last week she would be backing Van Hollen.

"I've been clear as well that I don't think that Sen. Schumer is best positioned to be our next leader. I'm encouraged that people like Chris Van Hollen got in the race, and because I've been clear that I wasn't supporting Schumer, I will be supporting Chris Van Hollen," Slotkin stated in a video posted to social media.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

"But I think no matter the outcome, it's going to be imperative for our leaders to demonstrate how they're going to incorporate that next generation, and what big and bold ideas, specifically, they're going to put forward in the first 100 days," she said.

Van Hollen shared Slotkin's post on X and wrote, "@SenatorSlotkin & I agree: the American people spoke, and we need new leadership in the United States Senate. Now is the time to act boldly, and we’re going to work together to deliver results."

item.title: MAC admits that officials incorrectly cost Kent State touchdown with blown call against Eastern Michigan
item.description: The Mid-American Conference admitted officials erred overturning Kent State's touchdown against Eastern Michigan, citing insufficient video evidence.
item.content:encoded:
Officiating in college football has become a major, major problem.

Earlier this season, the Michigan Wolverines miraculously escaped against Western Michigan thanks to a controversial second being added to the game clock due to incorrect replay review procedures. While the MAC initially accepted the results, they then issued a statement criticizing how the situation was handled.

The Big 12 Conference admitted to several officiating mistakes, most of which benefited the BYU Cougars. During their game against Notre Dame, the referees failed to notice that the Irish should have had one second left to try and pull off a comeback win.

CLOCK CONTROVERSY: NCAA SAYS OFFICIALS BOTCHED REPLAY PROTOCOL IN MICHIGAN'S WIN OVER WESTERN MICHIGAN

"Following the Big 12's review of the final play of Saturday's Notre Dame-BYU game, it was determined that time remained on the clock when the ball hit the ground and the play was incorrectly cleared by the replay officiating crew," they explained in a statement. "The Conference will conduct a complete review of its end-of-game officiating process in advance of next week's games."

Then there was the inexplicable handling of the end of the BYU-UCF game, where a facemask penalty flag was picked up, and the Knights were incorrectly assessed a 10-second runoff at the end of regulation. Amazingly, the next week, the Cougars were given a touchdown on a fumble recovery that should not have been allowed thanks to a blown whistle.

In the SEC, the Texas-Missouri game featured several contentious calls that went the Longhorns' way, including the most absurd, awarding Arch Manning and Texas a first down on a fumble, though his arm was clearly moving forward. Analysts were so critical of the officiating in that game that they drew a rebuke from Greg Sankey afterward.

Notre Dame-Miami came down to what looked to be a massive touchdown catch for the Irish, waved off as incomplete. Those are just a few examples. And now we have another one. This time, ironically, involving MAC officials.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

During some recent late-night MACtion, a Kent State appeared to come down with a walk-off touchdown catch to beat Eastern Michigan. After an insane five-minute review process, the officials overturned it, based on, well, not much, and handed the win to the Eagles.

THE ABSOLUTE WORST CALL OF THE COLLEGE FOOTBALL SEASON HAPPENED LAST NIGHT WHILE YOU WERE SLEEPING

On Wednesday, the conference admitted that the officials erred in making the call and that Kent State should have won the game.

In a statement, they acknowledged that there was "insufficient video evidence to overturn the ruling on the field."

"The video evidence did not meet the clear and obvious standard required to overturn the ruling on the field," they added. "The decision to overturn the touchdown was incorrect, and the original ruling should have been upheld. The Mid-American Conference recognizes the significance of this error and regrets its impact on the outcome of the game. Our student-athletes, coaches, institutions and fans deserve the highest standards of officiating. The Conference remains committed to those standards and to maintaining the competitive integrity of our contests."

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

Kent State head coach Mark Carney told ESPN that he was "heartbroken" by the outcome.

"In 25-plus years of playing and coaching college football, I have never felt the disappointment I felt last night postgame," Carney said. "Heartbroken for our players and staff who pour so much of themselves into what we do - especially those playing their last game of college football. We are extremely proud of the way our young men represent Kent State, our football program, and themselves."

Man, it doesn't get worse than that. Having the outcome of a game be directly affected by the officials making the wrong ruling. You have to feel terrible for Kent State players, fans, and coaches. And frustrating that officiating continues to be such a disaster when there's no excuse for it to be. Gotta be better and let the MACtion dictate the outcome, not the refs.

item.title: ‘Charlie Brown’ voice actor received zero residuals for nearly 50 years due to banned ’70s contract
item.description: Todd Barbee, the voice of Charlie Brown in "A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving," says he got no residuals for decades until SAG-AFTRA renegotiated old contracts.
item.content:encoded:
Good grief — it turns out the voice of Charlie Brown didn't even make peanuts in residuals.

Todd Barbee was just 10 when his father's connection to producer Lee Mendelson landed him the iconic role of Charlie Brown in 1973's "A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving." Generations grew up watching his performance on network TV, yet Barbee, now 63, revealed to host Joseph Sibilia on his podcast, "Nostalgia Tonight with Joe Sibilia," that he didn’t receive residual checks until about six years ago.

"Aside from the bountiful residuals I'm sure you've collected for the last 50-plus years, what has been the most rewarding part of being a part of the 'Peanuts' legacy?" Sibilia asked Barbee.

‘BRADY BUNCH’ CAST MADE NEARLY NOTHING FROM DECADES OF RERUNS, EVE PLUMB CLAIMS

"Well, let me correct you on one front," Barbee replied. "... We were actually under an old contractual relationship from the '70s that is no longer allowed by Screen Actors Guild and AFTRA, which is American Federation of Television and Radio Artists. The contract was a buyout, and that is not allowed by the unions anymore. I think it was overturned in the '80s."

"So, we did not receive any residuals at all," Barbee noted. "In fact, I didn't receive a single residual until about six years ago."

The initial gig paid "pretty handsomely" at the time "in 1970 dollars." He used his paycheck to help his mother buy the house that she still lives in to this day after his parents divorced. However, he didn't see any residual checks, no matter how massive the special became as a holiday tradition.

WATCH: CHARLIE BROWN VOICE ACTOR TODD BARBEE WENT DECADES WITHOUT ‘PEANUTS’ RESIDUALS

"Peanuts" made its debut on Oct. 2, 1950. The travails of the "little round-headed kid" Charlie Brown and his pals eventually ran in more than 2,600 newspapers, reaching millions of readers in 75 countries.

According to Barbee, everything changed after union renegotiations around streaming rights following Apple TV's acquisition of the "Peanuts" catalog. The streaming service obtained the exclusive rights to the "Peanuts" catalog in 2020, including the widely beloved "A Charlie Brown Christmas."

"... During the big strike, writers' strike and everything that happened about five or six years ago ... Screen Actors Guild renegotiated some of these things," said Barbee. "And they determined Apple TV right now actually has the entire 'Peanuts' catalog. And what Screen Actors did [was say], 'Look, that doesn't have anything to do with these old contracts. That was for broadcast television. You're a streaming service. And as such, you need to pay these people current residuals.'"

"So now, I do make some money every year off all the specials," said Barbee. "It's not giant amounts of money, but you know, it's significant. And I look forward to getting that check every year."

Fox News Digital reached out to SAG-AFTRA, Apple and Peanuts Worldwide for comment.

From 1972 to 1974, Barbee voiced several "Peanuts" characters across five different TV specials. Because producers insisted on authentic kids' voices rather than adults imitating children, every young actor received what Barbee called a "Dear John" letter.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"One of the things that's very interesting about all the characters in 'Peanuts' is you got a 'Dear John' letter the moment your voice changed," he told Sibilia.

"... They were looking for kids whose voices hadn't changed. They really ... had an idea about the intonation and the character of the voice, and it needed to be a kid's voice. And so, there was an audition. They wanted to do a number of specials at the same time, one after the other. They were talking about Thanksgiving and Easter and others."

"I was about 10 then, maybe a little bit more than 10 years old," Barbee reflected. "And the next thing you know, they had me voice for Charlie Brown and they selected me."

After leaving acting behind, Barbee pivoted to graphic, commercial, and site design in the San Francisco Bay Area. In a fitting nod to "Peanuts" creator Charles Schulz, an avid hockey fan who built a famous ice arena in Santa Rosa, Barbee's design work includes the site plan for Fisherman's Wharf's observation wheel and its inaugural seasonal outdoor ice-skating rink. 

For decades, Barbee kept his "Peanuts" past under wraps.

"People that were in the know knew about it," said Barbee. "But many of the people that I've known throughout the years, I never talked about it. It was just not a big thing for me. It was just kind of a funny insider thing. And if you really got to know me, you either found out, maybe I dropped it or a friend mentioned it."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Today, Barbee says the greatest reward is knowing his voice still brings holiday cheer into homes across America half a century later.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"... I get this fan mail with frequency still to this day," said Barbee. "And that just always puts a smile on my face because I realize how this character has influenced so many people's lives over the course of, you know, half a century. And there's something very, you know, very special about that. So, it's cool to be involved in that."

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Aaron Rodgers vs Mike McCarthy: Timeline of beloved Super Bowl duo's descent into baffling NFL soap opera
item.description: Aaron Rodgers accused Mike McCarthy of falling asleep in meetings and missing walkthroughs on "The Pat McAfee Show" before the Steelers released him.
item.content:encoded:
Aaron Rodgers and Mike McCarthy made divorce the theme of this Thanksgiving.

Rodgers accused McCarthy of falling asleep in meetings, skipping team activities and harboring resentment over his 2018 firing in Green Bay, even claiming he had covered for his coach for years. McCarthy denied holding a grudge against Rodgers.

But long before their reunion in Pittsburgh imploded, the two men shared a complicated 21-year history that included an NFL Draft rejection, a Super Bowl triumph, public confrontations and seemingly heartfelt reconciliations.

Before Rodgers ever played a snap in the NFL, McCarthy helped deny him a childhood dream.

McCarthy was the San Francisco 49ers' offensive coordinator in 2005 and helped evaluate Rodgers, a Northern California native and lifelong 49ers fan who starred at nearby Cal. But San Francisco selected Utah quarterback Alex Smith with the No. 1 overall pick, leaving Rodgers to endure an infamous, hours-long wait in the NFL Draft green room on national television before Green Bay selected him 24th overall.

Former 49ers head coach Mike Nolan acknowledged McCarthy's influence on the decision in Ian O'Connor's 2024 biography of Rodgers, saying McCarthy was the most knowledgeable member of the group when it came to quarterbacks.

"It was my first head coaching job, and Mike was the guy who was most knowledgeable on quarterbacks of the group, and as a group that's what we decided. … He had a lot to do with picking the other one (Smith), and in the end he got the one (Rodgers) that he didn't pick, and it elevated his career," Nolan said in the book.

McCarthy was quoted in the book giving his side of that story, saying "I was the offensive coordinator, and I did express my opinion. But those selections are made by a group of people, and ultimately a lot of information goes into that. I thought both quarterbacks were very young, talented guys who you could win with."

Three years after passing on Rodgers in the draft, McCarthy publicly admitted he had misjudged the quarterback.

"Aaron is extremely athletic," McCarthy said. "I've said it before, I did not evaluate him properly in the movement phase at quarterback coming out of college. I did not see the athletic ability that I have been able to witness since we've worked together."

McCarthy had spent the previous two seasons developing Rodgers and was preparing him to take over as the Packers' starting quarterback following Brett Favre's retirement.

But when Favre came out of retirement that summer, Rodgers suddenly found himself facing the possibility of having to compete for the job he had waited three years to inherit.

Rodgers was met with boos from some Packers fans during the team's annual Family Night scrimmage on Aug. 3, the night Favre returned to Green Bay.

"They're booing all of us, probably me mostly. So, yeah, I take it personally," Rodgers told reporters that night.

McCarthy met privately with Favre for several hours the following evening. The meeting ran so long that the Packers canceled a scheduled press conference, and a team spokesman said McCarthy had not spoken to Rodgers that day, according to The Washington Post.

But McCarthy ultimately stood by Rodgers, publicly defending the young quarterback amid the controversy.

"He's done everything right to this point, so why would I put him through any more than he needs to go through?" McCarthy told reporters Aug. 5.

Favre was traded to the New York Jets the following day.

Around 2010, Rodgers and McCarthy began meeting privately on Thursday afternoons after practice.

"Some about football, but a lot about life. Lessons, thoughts and dreams," Rodgers recalled in December 2018, shortly after McCarthy was fired.

McCarthy reminisced about those meetings during a 2019 interview with NFL.com, acknowledging how much he missed those conversations. In November 2022, McCarthy revealed how those encounters would typically end.

"And it always ended with a hug and, 'I love ya,'" McCarthy told reporters.

Their partnership reached its pinnacle on Feb. 6, 2011, when the Packers defeated, ironically, the Pittsburgh Steelers 31-25 in Super Bowl XLV.

Rodgers was named Super Bowl MVP the following night. Neither man has won another Super Bowl since.

McCarthy briefly handed his play-calling duties over to Rodgers during the Packers' 2011 regular-season finale against the Detroit Lions.

With Rodgers resting ahead of the playoffs, McCarthy tasked him with calling the offensive plays for backup quarterback Matt Flynn throughout the first half. Flynn went on to set franchise records with 480 passing yards and six touchdown passes in a 45-41 victory.

"He's got a bright future in coaching," McCarthy joked to reporters the following day.

McCarthy expanded Rodgers' play-calling responsibilities in 2012 before scaling them back in 2013, determining he had put too much responsibility on his quarterback.

The tension between Rodgers and McCarthy spilled onto the sideline on national television during a Week 3 game against the Cincinnati Bengals.

Rodgers had been stopped at the 1-yard line on a third-down scramble in the second quarter, prompting the Packers to settle for a field goal. An animated Rodgers confronted McCarthy on the sideline over his play-calling, and Fox's television cameras captured defensive tackle B.J. Raji extending an arm between the two men as they argued.

The Packers went on to squander a 16-point second-half lead, losing 34-30. Rodgers threw multiple interceptions in a regular-season game for the first time in nearly three years.

McCarthy downplayed the confrontation after the game, even suggesting Rodgers' willingness to express his frustration was something he admired about his quarterback.

"He's competitive, man. That's what I love about him. I don't think it's that big of a deal," McCarthy told reporters.

Rodgers confirmed the argument was over play-calling but refused to disclose the specifics of what was said between them.

Two days later, Rodgers addressed the incident again on his ESPN Milwaukee radio show, insisting the two had resolved their disagreement and emphasizing their history of success and mutual respect.

"There's a lot of competitiveness and passion on both sides, and every now and then that passion collides," Rodgers said.

As Rodgers and McCarthy prepared for another playoff run after a 12-4 regular season, some of Rodgers' teammates revealed how intense the relationship between the two men could get behind the scenes.

Former Packers backup quarterback Seneca Wallace told NFL.com that McCarthy would become frustrated when Rodgers independently called plays without his knowledge, sometimes prompting the coach to blurt out, "What the f---? What is he calling?"

Wallace estimated Rodgers could call 40 of the team's 70 offensive plays in a given game.

"Coach McCarthy always talks about alpha dogs — well, they're like two alphas going at it," Packers linebacker and close friend of Rodgers, A.J. Hawk, told NFL.com.

Rodgers suggested their occasional confrontations had only strengthened their relationship.

"But I think we both know each other well enough that the last thing that either of us want to do is disrespect each other," Rodgers said.

Speculation about tension between Rodgers and McCarthy became so widespread among Packers fans that the two agreed to give separate interviews to Green Bay Press-Gazette reporter Pete Dougherty to address their relationship.

The Packers had just finished their worst regular season in total offense since Rodgers became the starting quarterback.

"This is the most frustrated I've ever seen him," McCarthy said of Rodgers.

McCarthy suggested he was uniquely positioned to challenge Rodgers, while the quarterback maintained their disagreements had always been constructive and rooted in mutual respect.

Just two days after the interviews were published, television cameras captured Rodgers and McCarthy sharing playful moments on the sideline during a 35-18 playoff victory over Washington.

McCarthy acknowledged the significance of those images amid the speculation about their relationship.

"I enjoy our relationship. I guess it's good everybody got to see good clips," McCarthy told reporters the following day.

Four years after their heated sideline confrontation in Cincinnati, another game against the Bengals produced an awkward moment between Rodgers and McCarthy.

CBS cameras captured Rodgers looking toward the Packers' sideline and appearing to mouth, "Stupid f---ing call!" twice after taking a sack late in the third quarter.

When Rodgers arrived for his individual meeting with McCarthy the following week, the head coach already had footage of the incident pulled up on a screen, according to a November 2018 Sports Illustrated report.

McCarthy had worked with Rodgers early in his career on controlling his body language when frustrated. More than a decade into their partnership, the two reportedly revisited those lessons.

The Packers ultimately won the game 27-24 in overtime.

Alex Van Pelt, who played quarterback at the University of Pittsburgh while McCarthy was a graduate assistant there, had served as Rodgers' quarterbacks coach since 2014.

But McCarthy brought in a new quarterbacks coach after Van Pelt's contract expired following the 2017 season.

Rodgers publicly expressed his displeasure during an appearance on ESPN Radio's "Golic and Wingo" during Super Bowl week.

"Well, my quarterback coach didn't get retained," Rodgers said. "I thought that was an interesting change, really without consulting me."

McCarthy had previously characterized Van Pelt's departure as a mutual decision, as the assistant had aspirations of becoming an offensive coordinator.

However, several sources close to the Packers later told Sports Illustrated they believed McCarthy had come to view Van Pelt as a threat because of his close relationship with Rodgers.

Van Pelt ultimately took another quarterbacks coaching job with the Cincinnati Bengals.

Rodgers was celebrating his 35th birthday on Dec. 2, 2018, when he learned McCarthy had been fired.

"I was at home with my folks in town for my birthday. When I found out, I was as shocked as many of you were, I'm sure," Rodgers said.

The Packers had fallen to 4-7-1 after an embarrassing 20-17 home loss to the Arizona Cardinals earlier that day, prompting the franchise to abruptly end McCarthy's tenure after nearly 13 seasons.

Fox Sports' Terry Bradshaw suggested Rodgers was responsible for McCarthy's firing, an assertion Packers president Mark Murphy publicly disputed the following day.

Rodgers also pushed back against speculation about their deteriorating relationship, revealing that he and McCarthy had actually spent more time talking to each other during the 2018 season than in previous years.

But it was a chance encounter outside Lambeau Field in the days after the firing that made the separation particularly surreal for Rodgers.

While driving to work one morning, Rodgers looked across an intersection and spotted McCarthy sitting in his truck. Rodgers recounted the encounter to reporters four years later.

"It was a really weird feeling," Rodgers said, recalling the moment it finally sank in that McCarthy was no longer his head coach.

Four months after their separation, an extensive Bleacher Report investigation exposed alleged dysfunction between Rodgers and McCarthy dating back to the early years of their partnership.

The report alleged McCarthy would miss team meetings to receive massages in his office, while Rodgers had privately questioned his coach's football intelligence and harbored resentment dating back to the 2005 NFL Draft.

McCarthy denied the massage allegations, calling them "utterly absurd."

But perhaps McCarthy's most prominent defender was Rodgers himself.

During an April 8 appearance on ESPN Wisconsin's "Wilde and Tausch," Rodgers characterized the report as a "smear attack," defended McCarthy's character and revealed he regretted publicly criticizing his coach's game plan after the Buffalo game the previous September.

"I love Mike McCarthy. He's a great man, he has a huge heart," Rodgers said.

Rodgers also pointed to his decision to sign a four-year, $134 million contract extension in August 2018 as evidence against the notion that he disliked playing for McCarthy, arguing he had anticipated spending the remainder of his career with him.

Rodgers even made a personal plea to Packers fans in Green Bay, where McCarthy and his family still lived.

"If you see Mike, shake his hand. Tell him thanks for the memories. Tell him thanks for the coaching job that he did," Rodgers said.

Four years after their separation, McCarthy returned to Lambeau Field to face Rodgers as opponents for the first time, with McCarthy coaching the Dallas Cowboys.

The two men had been communicating more frequently over the previous year, according to Rodgers, and exchanged compliments publicly in the days leading up to the game.

Television cameras captured Rodgers and McCarthy sharing an embrace during pregame warmups. But Rodgers later revealed the two had arranged a private meeting well before kickoff, away from the cameras.

"We had a really beautiful conversation before the game. Just really thankful for that time," Rodgers told reporters.

Rodgers then led the Packers to a 31-28 overtime victory, overcoming a 14-point fourth-quarter deficit and spoiling McCarthy's return to Green Bay.

After the game, an emotional and visibly frustrated McCarthy was less inclined to discuss the sentimental significance of his homecoming.

"I'm not trying to be rude, (but) I'm humble pied out," McCarthy told reporters.

Rodgers played a role in bringing McCarthy back to the NFL.

Following Mike Tomlin's resignation in January, Rodgers encouraged Steelers general manager Omar Khan to interview McCarthy, later admitting he had not expected the franchise to seriously consider his former coach.

During a March 4 appearance on ESPN's "The Pat McAfee Show," Rodgers learned that McAfee had also vouched for McCarthy after working with him as a regular guest on the show throughout the 2025 season. McAfee specifically praised McCarthy's preparation and work ethic.

Rodgers agreed with McAfee's assessment and expressed enthusiasm about McCarthy returning to his hometown to coach the Steelers.

Meanwhile, McCarthy returned to Lambeau Field on March 23 for a tribute to former Packers president Bob Harlan. When asked about potentially coaching Rodgers again, McCarthy said, "Yes, it would be a great story."

Rodgers officially re-signed with Pittsburgh on May 18, committing to playing his final NFL season under McCarthy.

Rodgers revealed two days later that sitting in McCarthy's first morning meeting had transported him back to being a 22-year-old quarterback in Green Bay.

"It's like a pinch-me moment," Rodgers said.

However, Rodgers acknowledged that McCarthy had changed aspects of his offense during their eight years apart and indicated there were certain elements of his coach's play-calling terminology he would push back on.

Just six months after describing his reunion with McCarthy as a "pinch-me moment," Rodgers publicly aired grievances against his longtime coach that dated back more than a decade.

The Steelers announced late Tuesday night that Rodgers would be inactive for Friday's game against the Denver Broncos in favor of Mason Rudolph. Rodgers claimed he learned of the decision during a phone conversation with teammate Pat Freiermuth, not from McCarthy himself.

During an explosive appearance on ESPN's "The Pat McAfee Show" the following afternoon, Rodgers accused McCarthy of repeatedly falling asleep in meetings, missing walkthroughs and failing to adequately prepare for games.

Rodgers said one of the breaking points came during halftime of Pittsburgh's 19-16 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles on Sunday, when McCarthy mistakenly broke down the team's huddle by saying, "One, two, three, Packers."

But Rodgers' allegations extended well beyond their brief reunion in Pittsburgh. The quarterback claimed similar issues had persisted throughout much of their time together in Green Bay.

"I covered for him for a lot of years and we worked around it," Rodgers said.

Rodgers also alleged McCarthy had privately expressed resentment over his firing in Green Bay eight years earlier, believing Rodgers was responsible for it.

Ultimately, the relationship came to a head over the same issue that had repeatedly generated friction between the two men over the previous 15 years: play-calling.

Rodgers said he told McCarthy the Steelers would be better off with someone else calling offensive plays and asked to be released if the team was unwilling to make that change.

The Steelers officially released Rodgers on Wednesday afternoon.

McCarthy subsequently told reporters the quarterback had issued an ultimatum that was "clearly out of his job description." He acknowledged the embarrassing halftime incident in Philadelphia but denied harboring a grudge against Rodgers over his departure from Green Bay.

After 21 years, two franchises and a Super Bowl championship together, McCarthy was once again the coach who decided to move forward without Aaron Rodgers.

item.title: UK shields fighter jets, contacts reservists in Cold War-scale push amid Russia threat
item.description: Wes Streeting says the United Kingdom is contacting former service members to update its strategic reserve as Russian sabotage rises across Europe.
item.content:encoded:
The United Kingdom is bolstering its military readiness amid growing threats from Russia, contacting former service members to assess its reserves as the Royal Air Force reportedly strengthens defenses against potential drone attacks.

Britain's Ministry of Defence has written to former service members to verify their contact information and military skills to ensure the country is prepared for a national emergency or potential conflict, Secretary of State for Defence Wes Streeting confirmed Friday.

The outreach comes as the International Institute for Strategic Studies warned Thursday that suspected Russian-directed sabotage across Europe could trigger a "mass-casualty event."

NATO WARNS PUTIN COULD STRIKE BEFORE EUROPEAN ARMY RESPONDS, POINTS TO US AS MILITARY MODEL

The think tank found that sabotage incidents rose 16% in the year through September 2026, with Germany and Poland accounting for more than half of the cases. Researchers warned that a major attack could spark calls for retaliation and divide European governments.

"I want the country to be alert, not alarmed," Streeting told BBC Radio 4's "Today" program.

"You can't not look at what's going on in Europe and not be concerned about a threat environment which has deteriorated in recent years and is sadly increasing," he said.

Streeting said the government needed updated records of its strategic reserve in case former service members were called upon to respond to a domestic disaster or overseas conflict.

He cited Russian incursions into Polish airspace, suspected Russian-sponsored sabotage across Europe and Iran-linked threats to British military bases.

Last week, a suspected Russian projectile landed in eastern Poland about 60 miles from a British-led military exercise. The incident happened the same day Britain's defense secretary and chief of the air staff visited troops.

INSIDE THE PENTAGON'S DOOMSDAY PLAN TO KEEP AMERICA FIGHTING IF GLOBAL WAR ERUPTS

"And so against that backdrop, against that threat environment, the government and the country has to be ready to face down those risks," Streeting said. "Because the more ready we are, the less likely we are to find ourselves in a conflict, in a war. That is my goal. That is the goal of this government."

The Ministry of Defence said in a news release it was contacting thousands of former military personnel this week as part of a drive to "strengthen the UK’s readiness and deliver on recommendations made in the Strategic Defence Review."

"Service Chiefs are writing to members of the Strategic Reserve, asking them to stay connected and update their details, providing Defence with a better understanding of the skills and experience it could draw upon if needed."

"In the coming months, Strategic Reservists will have the opportunity to volunteer for training and exercises, such as the UK’s participation in NATO’s flagship Steadfast Defender next spring."

The outreach marks the first time since the Cold War that Britain's defense ministry has contacted reservists on such a scale to encourage participation in military exercises, according to The Telegraph.

TRUMP’S PROPOSED RUSSIA DEAL RAISES NATO ALARM AS EX-COMMANDER WARNS PUTIN SEEKS INFLUENCE OVER EUROPE

Meanwhile, Britain's domestic intelligence agency, MI5, and the defense ministry have reportedly warned British companies supplying military equipment to Ukraine that they could be targeted by Russian saboteurs.

The Royal Air Force is strengthening security at military bases, using hardened aircraft shelters and installing anti-drone netting to protect exposed fighter jets, according to The Times.

The measures follow Iranian threats against military bases in England that prompted tighter security and the relocation of U.S. military aircraft.

Suspected drone incursions over European airfields have also heightened concerns about Russian aggression.

"We take the security of our bases, equipment and personnel very seriously and are always adapting to counter any potential threats," a Ministry of Defence spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

US MILITARY BASES ARE ‘ILL-EQUIPPED’ TO STOP DRONE SWARMS, TOP COMMANDER REVEALS AFTER RUBIO'S UAP WARNING

"This includes investing an additional £470 million to strengthen security at military sites, including better physical protection, surveillance and counter-drone capabilities.

"We have already invested £15 million in drone and counter-drone technology and introduced restricted airspace over 44 critical Defence sites."

The developments come as President Donald Trump said Thursday he had asked Russian President Vladimir Putin to "pull back all military aggression" against Europe, signaling a shift in tone toward the Russian leader, whom he called a friend last week.

Trump said he made the request during a meeting with Putin in China last week, adding that he believed it could help secure a deal to end Russia's war in Ukraine.

Trump's comments came a day after he hosted NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte in Florida. The two leaders issued a joint statement urging Russia not to expand its war in Ukraine.

"During my conversations in China with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, I spent a lot of time talking about the fact that I would like to see President Putin pull back all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe," Trump said on Truth Social.

item.title: Trump takes on Somali welfare dependency in Thanksgiving message, lays out who should stay in US
item.description: President Donald Trump says only 2% of Minnesota's Somali community should stay, claiming on Truth Social the rest should be thrown out to save the state.
item.content:encoded:
In a lengthy Thanksgiving message on Truth Social Thursday, President Donald Trump praised a small fraction of the Somali community, saying they should be allowed to remain in the United States, while calling for the immediate removal of those receiving government assistance while unemployed.

The holiday post mixed praise for "AMERICAN PATRIOTS" with criticism of the "Radical Far Left" and Minnesota’s Somali community, which Trump has frequently accused of public assistance fraud in the state.

"I want to thank the 2% of our Somalian population that have a job, and are actually willing to work, without receiving Government Assistance," Trump wrote in the post. "These are wonderful American ‘citizens,’ and should be allowed to stay in our Country, and celebrate Thanksgiving with us. The others should be thrown out, immediately, thereby saving the Great State of Minnesota, which has no chance if they are allowed to stay."

SOMALIS IN MINNESOTA UNLEASH FURY ON TRUMP AFTER FEDS RAID ILHAN OMAR'S DC HOME

Trump’s remarks echo ongoing criticism from some Republicans regarding public benefit usage and fraud cases within the community.

During a House Oversight Committee hearing in January, Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, highlighted data on government support programs, noting that 54% of Somali-headed households in Minnesota receive food stamps.

SNAP FOOD STAMP FRAUD HAS NEFARIOUS TERRORISM LINKS, TOP AGRICULTURE WATCHDOG WARNS CONGRESS

Elsewhere in the post, Trump claimed that "murderers, drug dealers, and criminals" — who he said illegally entered the U.S. from foreign prisons and mental institutions — have largely been deported.

"They are mostly gone now, brought back to their point of origin and, hopefully, living a beautiful and idyllic life, and promising, ideally, never to kill innocent people again," he wrote.

"We won’t have to worry about that, because they are GONE — but, Happy Thanksgiving to them anyway, even though from Faraway Lands," he added. "We miss you dearly, but you will never be back, and America will never allow what you have done to us to happen again!"

Secretary of State Marco Rubio also shared a holiday message on social media, with a video focused on opportunities provided by the U.S.

"We know how special this country is. It's the place that gave us freedom. It's a place that gave us opportunity. It's a place that's given our parents, our grandparents, and many of you the chance not just to do well in life, but to leave our children better off than ourselves," Rubio said in the video.

In the attached caption, he added, "Being an American is a gift unlike any ever afforded to any other peoples throughout human history — we have so much to be thankful for. Happy Thanksgiving."

item.title: Sylvester Stallone endured broke, lonely days cleaning lion cages before Henry Winkler changed his life
item.description: Henry Winkler recalls visiting Sylvester Stallone's blacked-out Lexington Avenue apartment, where the future "Rocky" star wrote scripts before fame.
item.content:encoded:
Before Sylvester Stallone became a Hollywood heavyweight, he was a broke, lonely actor living in a cramped New York City walk-up apartment with few friends to lean on — until Henry Winkler came along.

In his memoir, "The Steps," the "Rocky" icon recalls crossing paths with the future "Happy Days" star on the set of 1974's "The Lords of Flatbush." Though Stallone joked they were polar opposites — Winkler, a Yale graduate, and Stallone from "the college of what's the matter [with] you" — the two forged an instant bond.

For Winkler, it didn't take long to see Stallone's fierce determination to make it in Hollywood. It was a drive he witnessed firsthand when he visited his co-star's home on Lexington Avenue for the first time.

SYLVESTER STALLONE'S ADVICE TO THOSE WHO ARE STRUGGLING 50 YEARS AFTER 'ROCKY' CHANGED HIS LIFE

"He was living there with his first wife and their bull mastiff, who had more slobber than the Atlantic Ocean," Winkler recalled to Fox News Digital.

"He painted his windows black so that he would never be bothered by what time of day it was. He wouldn't be influenced by time. Instead, he just wrote and wrote. And from the minute we met on the set of a movie in which we made no money whatsoever, you could see him. You could see his drive. You could see there was something so special, so funny, so articulate coming out of this, 'I'm going to eat you for breakfast.' And it only continued."

"If you listen to Sly Stallone, you quickly realize he's a philosopher," Winkler shared. "You would never put the two together, but it's true. And he's so open. His upbringing would put any man or woman down. It would put them in a corner shaking for the rest of their life. But his motto is 'keep on punching' and it's true. He kept on punching. And it's been an honor to be his friend."

WATCH: SYLVESTER STALLONE REFLECTS ON CHILDHOOD TRAUMA, ‘ROCKY’ AND WHY ‘TRYING’ MATTERS MOST

In his book, Stallone described how Winkler had to "step over a homeless guy while walking up five flights of stairs" just to see his "shabby place and get a glimpse into my world." Instead of being horrified, Winkler was impressed by the library of tattered books and a shelf holding about 15 screenplays. Stallone had been keeping busy writing. 

When Winkler picked up one of Stallone's scripts, he was stunned. Winkler urged Stallone to keep writing.

Stallone told Fox News Digital he never forgot Winkler's kindness and encouragement during a time when hearing "no" was the norm.

"You cannot get two people more different in every aspect," Stallone said with a laugh. "We were, as I wrote, an 'odd couple.' And yet, he gave me such confidence. He's an intellectual, and I didn't think of myself that way. I didn't see myself that way at all. When he saw the writing, he said, 'You wrote all this stuff?' I said, 'It's not good.' He then said, 'That's not the point. You did 15, 15 scripts. It's harder to make it as a writer than an actor. This is impressive.'"

Stallone wrote, "We were an odd couple. He was an intellectual Jewish kid from the Upper West Side who graduated from the Yale School of Drama — the real deal. I had to learn everything the hard way. We were anomalies in each other's lives. To see us together was like watching a zebra hang out with a buffalo. Still, we clicked, because Henry is a genuinely wonderful human being."

Years later, after scraping by in New York and taking odd jobs like working at a deli, ushering at a movie theater and cleaning lion cages at the Central Park Zoo, Stallone headed west. He and his then-wife, Sasha Czack, made the cross-country trip to California in hopes of finally getting his big acting break. But they knew no one on the West Coast and didn't have a place to live. Stallone wrote, "We had barely $500 left of the $830 we departed New York with."

But there was one person Stallone knew he could call: Winkler. By then, the actor had already moved to California and become a star on "Happy Days."

"When I came out to California, he was the only guy I knew," said Stallone. "It was comforting because, again, he was very complimentary and welcoming. He kept saying, 'Working with you on "Lords of Flatbush" helped me with The Fonz, playing a tough guy.' I kept telling him, 'No, man, you did that all on your own.' But he saw something in me, even before ‘Rocky.’ Yes, this was a long time ago, but that's how great of a guy he was. He still is."

"Really, our relationship goes back to 1972," Stallone said with a smile. "It's amazing. Again, we're so different, yet there's a bond there that he actually instigated. I was a loner, no doubt about that. And yet he would insert himself, talk to me, be very outgoing and witty. He wanted to be my friend. And he was from Yale. He didn't have to be my friend. But he genuinely cared. We bonded and it's terrific."

Stallone and Czack eventually settled into a rental in Encino for $300 a month. The house was barely 500 square feet and there was no grass or air conditioning. Still, Stallone said he was determined to make it big in Hollywood.

In the book, Stallone described first arriving at Hollywood and Vine. He had no idea that the nearby Walk of Fame would one day bear his name.

"That I would have a star there less than 10 years later, and only a few blocks away, still boggles my mind," he wrote.

item.title: 'One Job Away' campaign is helping SAG-AFTRA members meet work thresholds to keep health insurance
item.description: Actor Cheyenne Jackson’s “One Job Away" campaign helping fellow SAG-AFTRA members meet work thresholds to maintain health insurance
item.content:encoded:
A grassroots social media campaign led by actor and singer Cheyenne Jackson has helped fellow SAG-AFTRA members struggling during declining film and TV production earn enough to keep their union health insurance.

Jackson, known for his roles in "American Horror Story," "30 Rock" and "Glee," launched the "One Job Away" movement on Instagram last month to spotlight fellow performers struggling to earn enough to maintain medical coverage through the Screen Actors Guild-American Federation of Television and Radio Artists.

SAG-AFTRA requires members to earn at least $28,000 annually to qualify for health insurance, with four quarterly deadlines for meeting that threshold, depending on when they joined the union.

NEWSOM SAYS FILM TAX INCENTIVES ARE BRINGING HOLLYWOOD HOME BUT INDUSTRY EXPERTS WARN IT MAY BE 'TOO LATE'

For actors working job to job, meeting that requirement has become increasingly difficult as U.S. film and TV production contracts and healthcare costs rise.

"So the success of the project so far at last count is that eight actors have been hired directly and at least 12 to 15 have been pinned or called back or gotten really close," Jackson told Fox News Digital. He described an overwhelming response, including hundreds of direct messages from actors hoping to be featured, many of whom are just a few hundred dollars short of qualifying.

Among them is William Ngo, who was born and raised in Southern California but relocated to Philadelphia after work dried up following the pandemic and the 2023 SAG-AFTRA strike. Ngo, whose credits include The CW’s "The Vampire Diaries," HBO Max’s "The Staircase" and Apple’s "Bad Monkey," is just $500 short of qualifying for SAG-AFTRA health insurance.

Actress and stunt performer Marie Gibeault, whose credits include Netflix’s "The Four Seasons" and multiple commercials, is only $800 short of qualifying. Navy veteran, actor and voice-over artist Jonathan Medina needs one guest role to qualify by the end of the year.

ROB RIGGLE SAYS HOLLYWOOD WORK IS DISAPPEARING FROM LA: 'IT'S THE EXCEPTION NOW'

Actor Alejandro Cardenas reached out to thank Jackson after the campaign helped him book a small role that put him over the earnings threshold.

"After Cheyenne posted my picture and info, an executive from Lionsgate and friend of mine immediately called me and set me up into this job so I could make the money needed to reach the minimum to qualify for my health insurance again," Cardenas told Fox News Digital from the set he was working on in New Jersey.

The actors’ profiles share a common thread: dwindling opportunities in Hollywood during fewer scripted television orders, increased cost-cutting and the continued shift of production elsewhere.

TRUMP, SCHIFF FORGE UNLIKELY ALLIANCE AS HOLLYWOOD BLEEDS JOBS

Jackson previously described the industry’s struggles as "systemic" during an interview with The Hollywood Reporter.

"People that have been leads of television shows have worked for years and years and years, and you know their faces, and you know their work. This year, they’re like, ‘What am I going to do?’" he said.

Meanwhile, beginning Jan. 1, quarterly premiums and earnings thresholds are expected to rise by 1%, with additional annual increases of 1% to follow, according to terms negotiated in SAG-AFTRA’s latest contract with streamers and studios.

A petition calling for an audit of the union’s health plan has also gained traction among members.

SAG-AFTRA, which represents approximately 170,000 media professionals worldwide, has faced criticism over the nearly $1.1 million annual salary of its national executive director and chief negotiator, Duncan Crabtree-Ireland, as members struggle financially.

Fox News Digital reached out to SAG-AFTRA’s chief communications and marketing officer, Pamela Greenwalt, for comment. In response, a union representative provided a healthcare fact sheet and a membership termination sheet.

Jackson, who also performs onstage, has expressed a desire to discuss how the system works, noting that actors can have a strong earnings year followed by a lean one that leaves them ineligible for health benefits.

He told Fox News Digital that launching "One Job Away" was a way to pass along kindness he had received.

Last year, for the first time in his 20-year career, Jackson found himself $6,000 short of meeting the health insurance eligibility requirements. Actress Kathy Bates, who had worked with him on "American Horror Story," arranged for him to have four speaking lines on her CBS series "Matlock." The work was enough to qualify him and his family for coverage.

"I really did nothing," Jackson said of launching "One Job Away." He added that several peers, including actresses Jamie Lee Curtis and Sarah Paulson, have reached out to ask how they can help.

"Just this helping one person makes this worth it," Jackson added, expressing disbelief at the outpouring of love he has received for trying to help.

item.title: EPA reports 'zero detection of airborne lead' day after Iowa lead azide detonation
item.description: The EPA reports zero detection of airborne lead after the detonation of five tons of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa.
item.content:encoded:
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) said Thursday that its air monitors continue to report "zero detection of airborne lead throughout the region" after the detonation of a stockpile of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant.

The statement comes as the EPA said it collected more than 1,000 samples following Wednesday's controlled detonation of the bomb-making chemical in Middletown, Iowa. Nearly 1,600 air, water, soil and dust samples were taken beforehand to establish a baseline for measuring any potential environmental changes.

Around five tons of degraded lead azide were destroyed after being deemed unsafe and unstable, and there were concerns that a plume of potentially toxic dust could drift towards Missouri in the wake of the blast.

"Following the controlled detonation, EPA sampled homes, public parks with playgrounds, and every drinking water intake in the pre-detonation plume model. Today, EPA personnel and contractors will be specifically sampling schools, playgrounds, daycares, churches, and more in the region," the EPA said Thursday.

ARMY DETONATES TONS OF LEAD AZIDE IN IOWA AS MAP SHOWS DUST PLUME PROJECTIONS

"Partnering with the U.S. Department of Agriculture, EPA has collected samples from nearby farms both before and after the controlled detonation," it also said. "Extensive sampling of water in the Mississippi River watershed has been completed both before and after the controlled detonation."

The EPA added that "air cassettes that sample for lead will be replaced to continue sampling today," and that "soil and dust sampling is expected to conclude today."

ARMY DESTROYS 68 BARRELS OF DEGRADED LEAD AZIDE IN IOWA

"The Trump EPA will continue its presence on the ground for as long as needed to ensure the proper environmental monitoring is taking place following the successful controlled detonation," it concluded.

EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said late Wednesday that the controlled detonation "exceeded expectations in a big way."

"Great job by the Army, and others, in Iowa!!!" added President Donald Trump on Truth Social.

item.title: Ukrainian intelligence says North Korea paused missile deliveries to Russia amid friction over South Korea
item.description: North Korea paused ballistic missile and artillery shipments to Russia after friction over Moscow's outreach to South Korea, Ukrainian intelligence said.
item.content:encoded:
North Korea has temporarily halted shipments of ballistic missiles and artillery shells to Russia following diplomatic friction between the two allies over Moscow's outreach to South Korea, Ukrainian military intelligence said Thursday.

According to Ukraine's GUR military intelligence agency, North Korean Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui announced the freeze on KN-23 ballistic missile and artillery deliveries last month after Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrey Rudenko suggested Moscow would help de-escalate tensions between Seoul and Pyongyang, Reuters reported.

Choe demanded that Russia clarify its policy toward South Korea, GUR said, though Reuters noted it could not independently verify the report or confirm public remarks from either official.

PUTIN'S WAR DEATH TOLL REPORTEDLY TOPS 700,000 AS RUSSIA SCRAMBLES FOR RECRUITS

The reported pause also suspends Russian military flights over North Korea and stalls a Kremlin request to expand North Korea's troop deployment in Russia from roughly 8,500 to 50,000, according to the outlet.

Rudenko, who oversees Asian relations, said last month that Seoul had signaled interest in normalizing ties and resuming direct flights with Moscow once the Ukraine war ends.

Despite the reported freeze, North Korean troops remain active in Russia, with 11th Corps units serving in the Kursk region and a missile unit operating in Voronezh since mid-summer, GUR said. Russian President Vladimir Putin also hosted top Kim Jong Un aide Jo Yong Won at the Kremlin last week, where both men reportedly praised bilateral cooperation.

Meanwhile, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned on social media Thursday that Moscow is "completing preparations for a new massive strike" on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, logistics and critical services.

TRUMP'S HISTORIC SUMMIT WITH XI, PUTIN MARKS DIPLOMATIC MILESTONE, BUT BREAKTHROUGHS REMAIN ELUSIVE

Crews are already working to restore power in six regions after overnight Russian missile and drone strikes damaged an apartment building, a hospital and businesses, according to Zelenskyy, who also renewed appeals for U.S.-made Patriot air defense interceptors.

In Washington, President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social Thursday that he urged Putin during talks in China to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe, in the hopes that a deal can be made between Russia and Ukraine, and made quickly."

U.S. envoy Jared Kushner, who is mediating talks with Steve Witkoff, said on the MD Meets podcast that Putin has "shown restraint" by agreeing not to use nuclear weapons, though negotiations remain deadlocked over Ukrainian territory.

Ukrainian forces also struck a Russian military airfield and an oil pumping facility overnight, while Russia claimed it intercepted 343 Ukrainian drones.

item.title: Politics, money and Thanksgiving dinner: Just two words can help avoid argument
item.description: Dr. Joel Davis Brown says swapping "yes, but" for "yes, and" can keep Thanksgiving dinner talk civil as post-midterm politics turn tense at the table.
item.content:encoded:
As Americans across the country sit down to Thanksgiving dinner just weeks after Democrats' midterm sweep drastically reshaped the political landscape going into 2027, conversations about politics and the economy could turn tense.

Dr. Joel Davis Brown, a leadership expert, executive coach and author who studies how people communicate and navigate conflict, says swapping out the word "but" when discussing controversial topics can help keep the discussions civil.

"‘But’ shows disagreement," Brown told Fox News Digital. "It’s a way of telling the person that what they said should not be heard, and it really stifles conversation."

Instead, Brown suggests trying "yes, and." That doesn’t mean you have to agree, he said. Rather it signals that you’ve heard the other person and leaves room to share a different view. "‘Yes, I’ve heard you and I have a different opinion,’" Brown said. "We can listen to varying opinions."

FOOD PRICES ARE RISING BEFORE THANKSGIVING. AN ECONOMIST SHARES WAYS TO SAVE

If a hot-button topic comes up, Brown recommends asking the person to "tell me more about that."

The question, he says, can help you understand how someone arrived at their view instead of turning the exchange into a debate.

He also cautions against opening with "I disagree," which can put people "in an oppositional place" before they have fully heard one another. Rather than trading facts and figures to win an argument, he said, people may make more headway by sharing personal stories and listening to the experiences behind someone else’s opinion.

"If you’re going into these exchanges as looking to win an argument, maybe change your approach," Brown said. "Maybe instead of trying to win that argument, you try to understand the other person’s perspective."

BLACK FRIDAY DEALS ARE EVERYWHERE. HERE’S HOW TO SPOT REAL SAVINGS

Brown said it helps to decide in advance what you want from the interaction, whether that’s getting through the meal, building a relationship or persuading someone. That goal can shape how you respond.

Political topics aren't the only ones that can get tense when families come together.

For personal questions about marriage, children or other life choices, Brown recommends setting expectations before the gathering. Talk with family or friends about what would help everyone feel comfortable, and be clear about what you do and do not want to discuss.

Additionally, if a conversation becomes stressful, take a breath, sip water or step away from the table. Brown said people should know their own triggers and remember they are not responsible for managing every interaction.

He encourages approaching disagreements with empathy, which he described as listening to another person’s story without taking on their position.

Family members may not see eye to eye, he said, but the holiday can still be a chance to learn from one another.

"Look at these as learning opportunities," Brown said.

item.title: FlyDubai to resume Tel Aviv flights following attempted hijacking incident
item.description: FlyDubai will resume flights to Tel Aviv, Israel, on Dec. 3 under new security arrangements after the Sept. 30 attempted hijacking, reports say.
item.content:encoded:
FlyDubai announced Thursday it will resume flights to Tel Aviv, Israel, next week, ending a suspension in place following an attempted hijacking incident in late September, according to media reports.

A source familiar with the matter told The Times of Israel that the airline is being allowed back into Israeli airspace "under new security arrangements."

The development comes after Transportation Minister Miri Regev decided this week that FlyDubai flights to Israel can resume pending clearance from Shin Bet, Mossad and Israel's National Security Council, the outlet reported.

A FlyDubai spokesperson told Reuters that the flights will begin again on Dec. 3. FlyDubai flights to Israel have been suspended since FlyDubai Flight FZ1073 on Sept. 30, when a co-pilot allegedly attacked his captain.

FLYDUBAI CO-PILOT ALLEGEDLY PLANNED TO CRASH ISRAEL-BOUND JET AT BEN GURION AIRPORT

That plane was diverted to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, where it made a safe landing.

"Captain Smit Machchhar, the Indian captain of FlyDubai Flight 1073, fought back after being stabbed in the cockpit," according to the Israel Foreign Ministry. "Despite being severely injured, he managed to unlock the cockpit door – allowing Israeli passengers and the Emirati crew to intervene and save all the passengers."

FLYDUBAI PILOT SHOWED WORLD 'THE HIGHEST FORM OF COURAGE,' INDIA'S PM SAYS

Israeli broadcaster Channel 12 reported that Hamam al-Hammami told investigators he intended to continue Flight FZ1073 toward Israel as though nothing was wrong, obtain the necessary clearances to approach Ben Gurion Airport and then crash the aircraft into a building or another plane at the airport.

UAE Attorney General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi said investigators determined that the co-pilot attempted to carry out a terrorist act by attacking the captain with a crash axe and attempting to take control of the aircraft.

Let's agree that a snapshot in time isn't a full picture of what's happening and Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams might have learned that in September when he was caught on camera during a "Monday Night Football" game pacing the sidelines during the national anthem.

Casually moving here and there while the Soldier Field crowd and teammates on the Bears sideline stood for the Star Spangled banner earned Williams some online criticism – probably warranted.

And during "The Star Spangled Banner" the network cameras focused on the Bears quarterback for a few seconds.

Williams was standing in one spot, not pacing.

item.title: Nick Saban is suddenly singing a very different tune about winning national championships
item.description: Nick Saban says winning a national championship doesn't prove a conference is best, undercutting the SEC arguments as Big Ten teams claim playoff titles.
item.content:encoded:
Nick Saban is inarguably one of the best coaches in college football history. His resume is difficult to match, from turning the LSU Tigers around in the early-2000's, ultimately winning a BCS national championship, to making the Alabama Crimson Tide a force of nature throughout the 2010s.

His ability to get the most out of his players, keep up defensively as offenses changed and evolved over time, and find and improve assistant coaches turned the Tide into a juggernaut. It's easy to forget now, but until Saban's tenure, Alabama went from 1980-2007 without being ranked number one in the major polls.

After winning his first title in Tuscaloosa in 2010, Saban famously said that it wasn't the end, but the beginning of a new run for the Tide. He was right. They won five more championships, including the COVID-adjusted 2020 College Football Playoff.

HERE'S HOW BAD THE COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF'S SELECTION COMMITTEE RANKINGS ACTUALLY ARE

Nobody questions Saban's accomplishments, or that Alabama was a dynasty in the Saban era. But one of the most harmful consequences of that time, for the rest of the sport, was that his success created the perception that the SEC was head and shoulders above the other conferences.

Winning a title is the ultimate accomplishment, and a reflection on the rest of the conference, the thinking went. And that thinking permeated throughout college football and was used to justify giving the SEC the preferential treatment in the College Football Playoff poll that they enjoy today.

Now though? Saban has thoroughly undercut that argument, and the justification for the SEC's obvious benefits, by saying winning a title doesn't determine the best conference. Speaking on "The Pat McAfee Show," Saban said that all those years of the SEC fans saying Alabama's national championship wins made them the best conference in the country was wrong.

"Just because you win a national championship does not make and evaluate the level of your league," Saban said. "It means you had a really good team that was better than everybody else, but it doesn’t mean you necessarily had the best league from top to bottom. My argument with the SEC has always been the strength of the league, from top to bottom. I think that’s very clear this year."

Interesting!

We'll come back to whether he's right or not, at least regarding this season, but what this seems to be is a convenient reshaping of the narrative. If the SEC had won the last three titles, while having little "depth," the Greg Sankey-SEC Network promotional apparatus would be saying that winning a championship is what matters most. But when the Big Ten wins three in a row, without the SEC even reaching the national championship game, it's a different story. Wonder why.

NICK SABAN SPEAKS TRUTH ON CFP EXPANSION: ‘THERE’S NOT 24 TEAMS’ THAT CAN WIN A NATIONAL TITLE, BUT MONEY WINS

Saban earlier this summer also accidentally undercut this very argument.

"I think the only reason people are talking about this is we dominated for so long, and we were so good, everybody makes a big deal out of being able to beat us," he said on SEC Network. "That doesn’t mean they’re better than us, and that doesn’t mean that just because you win the championship that you have a better conference. It just means you have one better team."

Ah, so they "dominated," he says. How did they dominate? By winning championships. How do we know? Because the SEC's depth during the Saban era was frequently worse than other conferences.

Let's look at the final AP poll after the 2015 season, one of Saban's championship winning seasons, as an example. The Tide finished No. 1, of course, but the next highest SEC team was...Ole Miss at No. 10. There were just two SEC teams in the top-15 of the final poll. Meanwhile, the Big Ten had four teams in the top-15, the ACC had three, and the Big 12 also had three. There were just three SEC teams in the top-20, the same number as the Pac-12.

So was the SEC the best and "deepest" conference that season? Or was it just that Alabama won the national championship, which automatically made them the best?

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

It's a similar story in 2017, when only three SEC teams finished in the top-17. The Big Ten had five. The Big 12 also had three. So which is it? Was the SEC the best because Alabama won? Because it certainly wasn't a deeper league.

In 2016, only one SEC team finished higher than No. 13 the final poll: Alabama. The Pac-12 had three teams in the top-13, the Big Ten had four. The Big 12 had two.

Most seasons, this is how it played out: Alabama was dominant, the rest of the SEC wasn't. Yet the chanting continued anyway, because they were winning championships. Now that they haven't, it's "we're the deeper league." Sure, Nick. And even with championships, going back as far as 2013, the SEC's won six championships, the Big Ten has won four, and the ACC's won three.

This season too, Saban's wrong. And we can use more objective measurements than the AP Top 25 poll to show it. ESPN's SP+, an opponent-adjusted ranking system based on offensive, defensive, and special teams efficiency and success rate, has seven Big 12 teams in its latest top-25 ranking. There are six Big Ten teams, five SEC teams, and three from the ACC.

So the Big 12 is the deepest conference right now, based on how teams would be expected to perform moving forward, based on opponent-adjusted success rate in the three facets of football. The Big Ten is the second deepest, and the SEC is third. When it comes to top-25 quality teams.

If you expand to the top-35, the Big Ten has a whopping 11 teams in that range, while the SEC has eight. And of course, their performance in last year's bowl season shows how much of the "depth" argument is just inaccurate perception. SEC teams were 0-3 against other Power 4 conferences in last year's playoff. They were 1-8 in bowl games. Alabama, the poster child for the SEC's unearned special treatment, were humiliated by Indiana in the Rose Bowl 38-3, after being gifted a spot in the tournament by an atrocious selection committee.

As is so often the case in college football, narratives shift based on what's most beneficial at the moment. The SEC this season is better at the top, but weaker in the middle, than the Big Ten or even the Big 12. Yet they still enjoy the benefits of perceived "depth" because of big stadiums and Lane Kiffin complaining. Or Greg Sankey's lecturing and propaganda tours. Or something. They haven't won a championship in the NIL era, while every school is paying players, yet still ride the coattails of Nick Saban's teams from 2009-2017. Though, of course, Georgia may very well win a title this year, in which case, the argument will switch back.

If the SEC had one good team and 15 bad ones, they'd be saying titles are what matters. If they had teams ranked 1-15 in SP+, and lost the championship, they'd be saying depth is what matters. The one constant? Whatever makes the SEC look best is the ultimate conference measurement.

item.title: Terrell Owens brings race into Aaron Rodgers conversation after QB torched Steelers coach before release
item.description: Terrell Owens claims a racial double standard in the NFL, saying he'd be called a cancer for Aaron Rodgers' behavior while Rodgers faces no backlash.
item.content:encoded:
NFL legend Terrell Owens brought race into the Aaron Rodgers conversation on Wednesday after the former Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback torched head coach Mike McCarthy and was released.

Owens, unprompted, went to his social media to offer his own blazing hot take about Rodgers bringing light to some of the things he was experiencing with McCarthy, who he said fell asleep during team meetings and broke a huddle down by saying, "1, 2, 3 Packers!"

"If I did some s--- like what Aaron Rodgers is doing, it'd be called conduct detrimental to the team, I would be called an insubordinate, I would be called a distraction, and I would be called a cancer, but why can he do that and he isn't getting crucified, but if I did it or somebody of color did, they would be getting raked across the coals," he said. "This is some privilege stuff right here.

WHERE DOES AARON RODGERS’ INTERVIEW WITH PAT MCAFEE RANK AMONG THE WILDEST IN SPORTS HISTORY?

"This is some double standard stuff right here because anybody knows I’d like to put myself in that situation since everybody has had an opinion about me and had so many negative thoughts about me because of the perception that the media has portrayed and pushed for so many years about me.

Owens said everything he did to start a media whirlwind was viewed negatively compared to what Rodgers did as he found his way out of the Steelers’ organization.

"Let’s just say this, you cannot deny there’s a double standard when it comes to the National Football League. It’s already said and it’s obvious in the world as a whole. But what I have been saying all along is that there’s a double standard and I was treated unfairly. I was viewed differently. My character was attacked. My character was tarnished based on s--- that media basically didn’t have true information from.

"So, now look at this situation, if that was me doing what Aaron Rodgers was doing, bro, I would be suspended without pay, I’d be talked about on every major network, I’d be viewed, like I said, probably as the worst person to ever put on a pair of cleats – I still am. But I urge you, people that listen to the media, and things that I’ve said and I’ve done throughout the course of my career, trust me people it wasn’t like that."

Owens said he began to understand he "couldn’t compete with the media." He said he still did what he did but did it under the "confines of the rules." He said that just because he wasn’t laughing, joking and being personable, it didn’t mean he "wasn’t a good person."

The former star pass-catcher did create his own media whirlwind during his time in the NFL.

Everyone remembers Owens working out in his driveway workout in the summer of 2005 as he looked to re-negotiate his contract with the Philadelphia Eagles and the not-so-subtle jabs at Donovan McNabb as their relationship frayed.

His greatness on the field wasn’t doubted, much like Rodgers. It was the circus that came along with that everyone held their nose about.

But, in his rant Wednesday, Owens urged people to talk to his former teammates to get their take on him.

"I’m telling you, this is how it is when it comes to the double standard of how White players get treated and how Black players get treated. And everybody’s like, ‘Oh, why does it always have to be race?’ That’s a good damn question. Why does it? Why does it have to be about race? Why can’t everybody be treated equal?"

He then made a claim about former San Francisco 49ers quarterback Jeff Garcia, who was once arrested on a DUI charge in 2004.

"When I was with the 49ers, I wasn’t treated as equal as Jeff Garcia. I knew I wasn’t. Jeff Garcia, I used to fall asleep in the meetings too. Guess what? Jeff Garcia used to come to practice inebriated."

OutKick reached out to Garcia for comment.

"So, if you’re going to think and talk bad about me because I’m saying that, say the same thing about Aaron Rodgers that’s going off on this rant about his coaches and things that were probably supposed to be kept in house. That’s what I’m talking about. There’s the double standard. Look at the color of the two players.

"This ain’t me trying to create no controversy. I’m just telling you the real on how it is and how I played and it’s still going on today. It’s going on today as a whole in this world. But like I said, there’s a double standard when it comes to us players. And I’ll leave it at that."

Rodgers’ interview on "The Pat McAfee Show" isn’t exactly being lauded. But it turned out some of the things he said was true. McCarthy admitted as much in his press conference.

In any event, Rodgers is set to become a free agent. The Steelers have a game on Friday against the Denver Broncos.

item.title: Bangkok oil refinery explosion injures at least 9, Thailand company monitoring air quality

item.content:encoded:
At least nine people have been injured in an oil refinery explosion in Bangkok, Thailand, on Thursday, with three in critical condition.

The explosion occurred at a Bangchak Corporation-owned facility, the company confirmed in a statement posted to Facebook.

The company also claimed it was able to control and extinguish a large blaze caused by the explosion within 30 minutes of the blast.

Additionally, it claimed monitoring showed no reduction in normal air quality.

"Since the incident occurred, the company has continuously monitored air quality in real time using automatic ambient air quality monitoring (AQM) stations, which the company has installed in the Phra Khanong, Bang Na, and Bang Nam Phueng areas to measure air quality around the refinery resulting from operations," the company wrote.

TWO INJURED AFTER EXPLOSION RIPS THROUGH CHEMICAL PLANT, SPARKING HAZMAT RESPONSE, SHELTER-IN-PLACE ORDER

"It was found that the air quality in the surrounding area of the refinery is within normal standards. Furthermore, at 5: 30 PM (17: 30 hrs.), the Pollution Control Department measured the air quality within a 3–4 km radius around the refinery—the same radial area—and confirmed that the measurement results are within normal standards," the statement added.

The company said it has also paused all production operations at the facility.
